Under each coin the string is equally likely to pass over itself in either of the two ways shown. What is the probability that the string is knotted after its ends are pulled?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: I see that the two small figures above respectively show two possible situations of the same crossing point: one line passes over the other line, or the line in the opposite direction passes over. In the main figure, there are three circular coins covering the three crossing positions of the rope; the three coins are arranged in a triangle and can be labeled as upper A, lower-left B, and lower-right C. The visible parts of the rope are connected into a triangular projection with three crossings, and the two free ends respectively extend out from below the lower-left coin and the lower-right coin. Then reason: the crossing under each coin has 2 equally likely ways of passing over or under, and they are independent of each other, so there are 2^3=8 possibilities in total. When enumerating these crossing states by A, B, C, only the two cases in which the three crossings are mutually consistent will form the standard trefoil knot figure: one is the trefoil knot, and the other is its mirror image. In the remaining 6 cases, at least one crossing is opposite to the other crossings, and after tightening and simplifying by planar deformation/Reidemeister moves, it will be eliminated into an unknot. Therefore the probability of forming a knot is 2/8=1/4.

raw_record.question_text: A piece of string is lying on the table. It is partially covered by three coins as seen in the figure. Under each coin the string is equally likely to pass over itself in either of the two ways shown. What is the probability that the string is knotted after its ends are pulled?

method.method_draft: Label the three covered crossings in the main image as top A, lower-left B, and lower-right C. From the image, first trace the visible portions of the string: the projection is the standard three-crossing triangular knot diagram with the two loose ends exiting below the two lower coins. Treat each coin as an independent binary crossing choice, using the two small crossing pictures above as the two possible over/under states. Enumerate the 2^3 = 8 possible assignments for A, B, and C. For each assignment, redraw the full crossing diagram and simplify by planar isotopy/Reidemeister moves after imagining the two ends pulled tight. The two assignments in which the three crossings are mutually consistent, giving the standard trefoil diagram, are knotted; the other six have a removable opposite crossing pair or simplify to an unknot. Therefore the probability is 2/8 = 1/4.

method.method_draft: Use a crossing-sign criterion rather than listing every case explicitly.
